content: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) conducted during the 1970s and early 1980s demonstrated that the polysaccharide serogroup A vaccine (SgAV) effectively prevented serogroup A meningococcal meningitis (SGAMM). However, subsequent non-randomized studies indicated that the duration of protection provided by the vaccine varied significantly depending on the age of the children receiving it. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the protective efficacy of the SgAV, the duration of its protective effects, its age-specific efficacy, and the impact of booster doses in children against SGAMM. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies published up to May 2010. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) as the primary source of evidence. Non-randomized studies were also considered, but only to address outcomes that were not covered by the RCTs. The methodological quality of the RCTs was rigorously assessed, and studies with a high risk of bias were excluded. Out of 12 eligible RCTs, four were excluded due to concerns about bias. Data from the remaining trials were pooled using the Exact method to evaluate vaccine efficacy. Additionally, 15 non-randomized studies were identified, but only two addressed objectives not covered by the RCTs, and both were deemed to have a high risk of bias. The analysis included eight RCTs, involving 236,760 vaccinated participants and 243,308 controls. The vaccine demonstrated a strong protective effect during the first year after vaccination, with a pooled efficacy of 95% (95% confidence interval: 87% to 99%). Protection appeared to extend into the second and third years post-vaccination, but the results for these time periods did not reach statistical significance. In Finnish children aged three months to five years, the vaccine was shown to be protective. This was the only trial that included booster doses for young children, but the study lacked sufficient statistical power to draw definitive conclusions about the impact of these booster doses. In low-income countries, the vaccine was also protective in children aged one to five years, but the efficacy within narrower age groups could not be determined due to limitations in the data. The authors concluded that the SgAV provided strong protection during the first year after vaccination in children over five years of age and in adults. However, the vaccine's efficacy beyond the first year could not be determined with precision. In children aged one to five years in low-income countries, the vaccine was protective, but the exact efficacy in this age group could not be established. Similarly, while the vaccine was effective in Finnish children aged three months to five years, the efficacy in more specific age subgroups could not be determined. The sample size was insufficient to draw reliable conclusions about the effects of booster doses.
